code-runtime.note: The copy-button runtime, mounted by DocContent only on pages that have a code frame. One delegated listener, one live region, and the two messages it announces — which are props now rather than string literals, because they are the only strings this package speaks to a screen reader at run time and they were English on every site in every language. If this grows past a kilobyte and a half it has stopped being one listener.

nav.note: One sidebar at every width: the shell, the navigation, the trigger and the scrim, plus the sidebar tree it wraps. It replaced a `<dialog>` drawer, and it is ~500 bytes heavier on purpose — `inert`, Escape, scrim dismiss and focus move-and-restore were the browser's while the navigation was a modal and are ours now. There is also a `ResizeObserver` re-reading the mode the stylesheet resolved, because `matchMedia` cannot answer a `@container` query. Raised once more for the sidebar’s marker column and the `icons` map it resolves names through — three inline glyphs and a lookup, no icon set. Growth past this means more behaviour moved out of the browser and into us, which is the direction to argue about. Raised again for the navigation's inner scroll box: the panel had to stop being the scroll container so it could hold edge shadows that do not travel, because an absolutely positioned child of a scroll container joins that container's scrollable overflow. That is one `<div>` — the smallest raise in this file, and the alternative was a shadow keyed to the page instead of to the navigation.

next-nav.note: `nav` plus `usePathname` and `next/link`. It should stay within a few hundred bytes of `nav`; a larger gap means Next wiring leaked into it rather than staying in this thin wrapper. Moves whenever `nav` does, and it did — for the drawer's scroll fix, the tree's translatable strings, then for the five behaviours that came back when the drawer went, and now for the sidebar's marker column and the icon map it threads through. Raised again for the navigation's inner scroll box: the panel had to stop being the scroll container so it could hold edge shadows that do not travel, because an absolutely positioned child of a scroll container joins that container's scrollable overflow. That is one `<div>` — the smallest raise in this file, and the alternative was a shadow keyed to the page instead of to the navigation.

next-search.note: `search-dialog` plus the Next router wiring. MiniSearch is NOT in here — it is `import()`ed on hover — so if this jumps by tens of kilobytes the lazy boundary has been lost. Moves with `search-dialog`, and did — for the result rows' glyphs. Nudged 20 bytes for the separator's cropped `viewBox`: `8 5 8 14` has less internal repetition than `0 0 24 24`, so the same eight characters gzip a little worse. No code was added — if this line ever moves by more than tens of bytes, something real did. Raised again for the result trail's names: a row reads `Getting started › Installation` rather than `getting-started › installation`, which is a lookup from route segment to title. The titles come from the navigation the layout already holds, NOT from a field on every search record — `search-index.json` is 46 KB gzipped on this package's own site and its README publishes that number.

search-dialog.note: The whole keyboard-first dialog: focus trap, combobox wiring, result rendering. The single largest thing this package ships to a browser, and the one worth defending line by line. Raised once for its chrome — a magnifier on the trigger and in the input, and the footer that replaced a standalone Close button: three key-caps, three verbs, and the dismiss control that is the only pointer route out of the dialog on a touch screen. Raised again for the result rows: a page/section glyph on every row and the two-column layout it buys. The icon is not decoration — with no icon a heading sat on the same column as the input's magnifier while the input's own text sat 24px right of it, so the dialog showed three left edges where a reader expects two and read as stacked levels rather than a list under a field. Which glyph is read off the `href` rather than a new index field, so the records did not grow; the paths are written out rather than imported from the sidebar, because reaching across would pull the whole navigation tree in to reuse one string. Raised again for the result trail's names: a row reads `Getting started › Installation` rather than `getting-started › installation`, which is a lookup from route segment to title. The titles come from the navigation the layout already holds, NOT from a field on every search record — `search-index.json` is 46 KB gzipped on this package's own site and its README publishes that number.

sidebar.note: A tree with disclosure groups and no router import. Raised four times, each time for a client-only necessity: 1.37 → 1.8 KB for scroll-into-view and the external-link icon; 1.8 → 1.9 KB when that scroll learned to run for the mobile drawer, where a `display: none` dialog had always left it with no scrollport to measure; 1.9 → 2.0 KB for the three strings this tree renders — the two disclosure verbs and the external-link suffix — which were hardcoded English under a `labels` prop claiming to be a site's whole translatable chrome; and 2.0 → 2.15 KB for the two type markers, a folder on every group and a page on every page. That last one is two inline SVG paths and the `icons` flag that turns them off, and it bought the only thing separating a category from a page in a tree where the two interleave — weight and a chevron were not enough to scan twenty rows. Then 2.15 → 2.25 KB to stop the tree collapsing behind the reader: a walk that names the groups holding the current route, so a navigation can open those and close nothing. The line it replaced was `setToggled({})` and cost nothing, which is the whole point — the cheapest possible reset was also the one that threw away every expansion the reader had made. If this approaches the dialog's 9 KB, the navigation has grown a feature that belongs on the server.

toc.note: A list plus one IntersectionObserver, and now the one thing an observer cannot answer. Raised once, 0.88 -> 1.03 KB, for the end of the document: `rootMargin` makes the top 40% of the viewport the region that counts as current, and at the foot of a page there is no scrolling left to bring a short trailing section into it — so it never lit up, while the heading above it stayed marked from inside the band. That is a passive scroll listener reading two numbers, plus the resolver both inputs now go through. It should stay the smallest client component here; the next growth to argue about is a *feature*, not a defect.

next-link.note: `next/link` with three props adapted, and nothing else. It exists so a consumer composing a shell by hand has something that type-checks under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` without a cast — so it should stay the thinnest thing in this list. Growth here means the adapter started having opinions, and the place for those is the component using it.

copy-page.note: The “Copy page” button. Holds no markdown: it fetches `/llms-full.txt` on click and slices this page out of it, so this is the control, the three icon states, the clipboard write and the slice — nothing that scales with the corpus. Raised once from 1.03 KB when the button moved off per-page `.md` URLs onto the corpus: the slice costs ~230 bytes and removed five steps of consumer wiring, two of which failed silently. Embedding each page's source in its own HTML was the other alternative, and it taxes every reader on every page load for a control most never press.

light.note: Prose-only pages: hast over the wire costs 20% more brotli than HTML would. This is the honest price of the architecture and the first number a skeptical reviewer asks for. If it exceeds this, restate the architecture argument — do not raise the budget.

heavy.note: Pages with code, tables and headings: 11.6%. The ratio improves as pages get heavier, because Shiki's token spans dominate both representations equally. Same rule as `light`.

shiki-multiple.note: Highlighting costs about 1.7x a render with the grammar excluded, measured idle (1.67-1.70 across runs). The budget sits well above that on purpose: this is the one timing metric here, and a contended machine moves it. Interleaving the two halves removed a systematic skew - separately-timed blocks reported 2.03x under load against 1.71-1.86x idle - but the residual noise is still +/-0.2x on a busy CI runner, in both directions. A budget inside that band fails for reasons the author cannot act on, which teaches everyone to raise a budget without reading it. A real regression here is a grammar or a transformer getting expensive, and that moves the number far past 2.1.
